anchor_text: Home-keeping youth have ever homely wits
summary: Valentine teases Proteus for staying home. 'Home-keeping' means staying at home, while 'homely' carried the older sense of 'plain, unpolished, limited' (not merely 'ugly'). The couplet echoes a Renaissance commonplace that travel broadened the mind: the educated Elizabethan gentleman was expected to widen his experience abroad.
detail: The proverb Valentine invokes — that staying home leaves the mind 'homely,' while travel ripens it — was a Renaissance commonplace, voiced at length in Lyly's Euphues (1578) and in the courtesy literature urging the young gentleman abroad. Onions glosses 'homely' in the sense 'plain, humble, unrefined' as current throughout the period. Valentine's joke is that love is the real 'chain' keeping Proteus provincial (line 3).

anchor_text: How young Leander cross'd the Hellespont
summary: Leander was a young man who loved Hero, a priestess on the far side of the Hellespont — the narrow strait between Europe and Asia (now the Dardanelles). Each night he swam it to visit her, guided by her lamp. Valentine cites his story as a 'shallow story of deep love,' punning on 'over shoes in love' (line 24): Leander was literally in over his head. The lovers became the classical byword for passionate, doomed devotion.
detail: Shakespeare encountered the tale through Ovid's paired love-letters (Heroides 18-19), the late-antique Greek poem attributed to Musaeus, and especially Christopher Marlowe's English epyllion Hero and Leander (1598). The Hellespont legend was widely known: Valentine's 'love-book' is exactly the kind of romance-anthology the story would fill. 'Over shoes' in love leads to the boot-pun at lines 25-27.

anchor_text: more than over shoes in love
summary: The two friends trade puns on the word 'boots.' 'Over shoes in love' and 'over boots' mean deeply in love — English proverbs for being in up to your neck. 'Give me not the boots' (line 27) means 'don't make a fool of me' (to 'give the boots' was to mock or rack someone). 'It boots thee not' (line 28) means 'it benefits you not' (OED: 'boot,' profit or advantage). Three meanings of one word in four lines.
detail: The proverb 'over shoes, over boots' meant 'in too deep to stop' — if your feet are already wet, wading deeper costs no more. 'To give the boots' as a form of mockery appears in Jonson and others. 'Boot' = profit or benefit survives in the idiom 'to boot' (into the bargain). Speed's verbal density throughout the scene is a deliberate contrast to the play's high-romantic register.

anchor_text: I am not Love
summary: Proteus says 'I am not Love' — meaning he is not the god Cupid (Love personified). Valentine retorts that Love is his 'master,' using the Elizabethan commonplace that lovers are the slaves or prisoners of Cupid. 'Yoked by a fool' (line 41) means enslaved by an irrational power: the fool is Cupid, traditionally depicted as a blind, capricious child.
detail: In Elizabethan poetry Cupid ('Love') was conventionally a boy-god who shot arrows without aim; his blindness explained why love appeared irrational. When Valentine says 'Love is your master, for he masters you,' he plays on the double sense of 'master' — Proteus's owner and the force that has mastered (overcome) him. The formula sets up the scene's sustained debate on love as a folly that 'vanquisheth' wit (line 36).

Cupid as 'Love' personified and the slave-of-love topos are central Elizabethan conventions, and the double sense of 'master' (owner/one who has mastered) is a straightforward reading of Valentine's line 40.

anchor_text: as in the sweetest bud / The eating canker dwells
summary: Both young men argue by analogy, trading versions of the same proverb: a 'canker' (a caterpillar or grub that eats rose-buds from within, also a kind of ulcer) destroys the flower at the height of its beauty. Proteus uses it to defend love — even the finest wits are prey to it. Valentine turns the image to accuse love: it blasts the bud before it can blow (blossom). This back-and-forth exchange of balanced arguments is called 'stichomythia' and was a standard device of academic debate.
detail: The canker-in-the-bud image was an Elizabethan commonplace; Shakespeare returns to it in Sonnet 35 ('As a canker in the fragrant rose') and Sonnet 95 ('How sweet and lovely dost thou make the shame / Which, like a canker in the fragrant rose, / Doth spot the beauty of thy budding name'). Both speakers here are doing what educated young men at the Inns of Court or university were trained to do: argue both sides of a proposition.

anchor_text: a votary to fond desire
summary: A 'votary' is someone who has taken a vow to serve a cause or deity — here, the deity Love. The word is semi-religious: a nun is a votary of God; a devoted lover is a votary of Cupid. 'Fond' in Elizabethan English does not mean 'affectionate' but 'foolish, infatuated' (its older sense, still present in 'fond of' only in weakened form today).

anchor_text: thou hast metamorphos'd me
summary: Once Valentine has left, Proteus soliloquizes that Julia has 'metamorphosed' him — transformed him the way gods transformed mortals in classical myth. The word comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses, the great Latin poem of mythological transformation. It is an early signal that Proteus's character will not hold its shape: the play's whole theme of inconstancy begins with his own admission that he has already been changed by love.
detail: Proteus's very name forecasts the theme. The sea-god Proteus could take any form to escape questioners; to be 'Protean' meant to be slippery and changeable. Here Proteus inverts the classical motif: he presents himself as the victim of transformation rather than its agent, blaming Julia. But the soliloquy also shows him abandoning his friend and his studies — a self-described change of priorities that the audience will watch accelerate when he reaches Milan.

Speed's clown logic always collapses into wordplay rather than truth.

anchor_text: a laced mutton; and she, a laced mutton
summary: 'Laced mutton' was Elizabethan slang for a prostitute (a woman with laces, i.e. stays, on her bodice, or 'dressed mutton'). Speed calls himself a 'lost mutton' (a lost sheep, a fool) and Julia a 'laced mutton' — a kept woman. The joke reduces Julia to a stock comic type and explains why she gave Speed nothing for his trouble: he insulted her.

Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) and Partridge (Shakespeare's Bawdy) both record 'laced mutton' as contemporary slang for a woman of loose character or a prostitute. Speed's use of it is a clown's misprision — he doesn't necessarily mean it maliciously, but it explains both the pun and Julia's cold reception. Linking it to 'lost mutton' (a stray sheep, a fool) is Speed's characteristic trick of running the animal/bawdy double sense simultaneously.

anchor_text: 'twere best pound you
summary: Proteus threatens to 'pound' Speed — meaning to shut him in a pound (a 'pinfold,' a small enclosure where stray animals were penned until their owners paid a fine). The exchange keeps the sheep-and-shepherd conceit running while piling up money-punning on top of it.

Speed's counterpun — 'fold it over and over / 'Tis threefold too little' — combines the folding of paper (letters) with the numerical sense of '-fold' and the monetary sense of 'pound' to claim he was underpaid for his errand.

anchor_text: that's noddy
summary: Proteus constructs the word 'noddy' from Speed's 'Nod + Ay.' 'Noddy' meant a simpleton or fool (like a nodding dunce), and was also the name of a card game. The joke is that Speed has been talking for several lines and his information amounts only to the word 'noddy' — i.e. he is a fool whose report says nothing. Speed immediately turns it back: he will accept 'noddy' as his wages since Proteus refuses to open his purse.

The entire passage is a virtuoso display of Speed's wit: he extracts a pun from every phrase Proteus gives him, while simultaneously refusing to deliver any useful information until he is paid.

anchor_text: you have testerned me; in requital whereof
summary: Speed has been tipped a 'tester' — a sixpenny coin (also called a 'testoon' or 'teston,' from the French word for the head of the sovereign stamped on it). 'Testerned' is Speed's invented verb: 'paid me with a tester,' i.e. cheaply tipped. He sarcastically 'thanks' Proteus for his generosity and announces he will carry no more letters.

Speed's mock-formal 'To testify your bounty, I thank you' layers the legal meaning of 'testify' (to witness, to give testimony) on top of 'tester,' giving Proteus both a receipt and a dismissal. 'Requital' means repayment or return — 'in return for which.'

anchor_text: the gentle Proteus
summary: Proteus was a sea-god in Greek myth who could change into any shape — lion, fire, water — to avoid answering questions. Shakespeare gives his faithless gentleman this name as a warning signal: a character named Proteus will not hold one shape, or keep one love. He will prove unfaithful to Julia and treacherous to Valentine.
detail: In Homer's Odyssey (4.351-570) Menelaus has to grip the sea-god Proteus fast through all his transformations before he will yield the truth. In Virgil's Georgics 4 he does the same for Aristaeus. 'Protean' became a byword for the shifty and unreliable. The naming is one of Shakespeare's clearest uses of a classical name as a character-emblem: while the constant Valentine (from Latin valens, 'strong') and the faithful Julia hold their form, Proteus changes with circumstance. The contrast structures the play's whole debate of love against friendship.

anchor_text: Fire that's closest kept burns most of all
summary: Lucetta deploys a proverb: a fire sealed from air burns more fiercely than one with an open draft. Applied to Proteus, it means that his silence is not indifference but suppressed feeling — the quieter a man's love, the more intense it may be. Shakespeare uses sententious proverb-forms like this to give servants a witty authority over their mistresses.
detail: The fire-and-air proverb was a commonplace of Elizabethan love discourse, exploiting the physics of combustion (a smothered fire grows hotter before it extinguishes) as a figure for pent-up desire. Lucetta's line is itself a counter-proverb to Julia's 'They do not love that do not show their love' (176), and the two women trade sententiae for two lines before the scene moves on — a set-piece of witty debate typical of Shakespeare's early comedies.

anchor_text: a goodly broker
summary: A 'broker' is a go-between or agent who conducts business on someone else's behalf. In the context of love, a broker arranged meetings and carried messages between lovers — a role that was respectable as a trade but disreputable when it meant aiding illicit courtship. Julia is sarcastically calling Lucetta a very fine 'agent' for letting herself receive a love-letter addressed to her mistress.
detail: By the late sixteenth century 'broker' in the sense of a love-messenger was sliding toward the more negative 'bawd' or procurer, and Julia's irony here is sharp. The same sliding sense of broker as both neutral agent and suspect panderer runs through much of Shakespeare's vocabulary for love-mediation. Compare Polonius's 'brokers' speech to Ophelia warning her that Hamlet's vows are 'brokers / Not of that dye which their investments show' (Hamlet 1.3), where the financial and sexual meanings entangle.

anchor_text: harbour wanton lines? To whisper and conspire against my youth
summary: 'Wanton lines' means immodest or lascivious verses. Julia accuses Lucetta of sheltering a love-letter that could corrupt her virtue ('against my youth'). For a well-born young woman in this period, receiving unsolicited love-letters was considered a genuine threat to her reputation and marriage prospects, so Julia's public indignation — even though she privately wants to read it — is the socially correct response.

detail: The Prodigal Son parable, the standard biblical text for a young man leaving home to seek his fortune, was well-known to any Elizabethan churchgoer. Launce invokes it sincerely, as the son leaving his weeping family, but botches the keyword. 'Prodigious' in Elizabethan English meant ominous, monstrous, or unnatural (OED s.v. 'prodigious' senses 1-2, citing portents and monsters), which accidentally tells its own truth about the departure. The malapropism is consistent with Launce's clownish speech throughout the play.

anchor_text: a Jew would have wept to have seen our parting
summary: Launce means this as a hyperbole: even someone with a reputation for being cold or unmerciful would have wept — so Crab's dry-eyed silence is especially shocking. In Elizabethan England, where Jews had been expelled since 1290 and were largely known through hostile stereotype, 'a Jew' functioned as a stock figure for hard-heartedness. The remark is a measure of comic excess, not a considered opinion.
detail: Jews were officially expelled from England by Edward I in 1290 and not formally readmitted until 1656. Elizabethan audiences knew Jewish characters mainly through stage caricature (Marlowe's Barabas, The Merchant of Venice's Shylock) and Protestant polemic that cast Jewish 'hardness of heart' as a theological category. The phrase 'a Jew' as a byword for callousness or avarice appears routinely in the drama of the period. Launce's comparison is purely comic hyperbole: even this stock figure of literary unmerciful-ness would have cried, yet Crab shed nothing.

The 'hole in it' is also a bawdy set-up that Launce declines to pursue, keeping the scene at the level of broad family comedy.

anchor_text: the unkindest tied that ever any man tied
summary: Panthino says Launce will miss the 'tide' (the moment the ship can sail with the current). Launce exploits the exact homophone: 'tied' (bound on a leash) means his dog Crab. The exchange runs from TLN 594 to 605 and adds a second punning pair when Launce stops Panthino mid-sentence ('lose thy tongue'), and Panthino's 'In thy tail!' (a rude joke at Launce's expense) lets Launce echo 'In thy tale' back — turning 'tale' (the long chain of losses Panthino is listing) against 'tail' (Panthino's insult).
detail: The tide/tied homophone and tale/tail homophone are both standard Elizabethan pun pairs. 'Tide' meant both the sea-current and an appointed time (OED s.v. 'tide' n. senses 3-4); Launce's dead-pan substitution of his dog's leash ('tied') for the nautical moment is a classic clown strategy of wilful literal-mindedness. Panthino's rhetorical chain ('lose the flood... lose thy voyage... lose thy master...') builds up for comic derailment, which Launce achieves first by literally stopping Panthino's mouth (physical comedy), then by the tale/tail exchange. 'Tail' as a bawdy or contemptuous term for the rear (OED s.v. 'tail' n. 7b) makes Panthino's 'In thy tail' an insult; Launce's 'In thy tale' turns the whole episode into a proof that Panthino's long-winded speech — his tale — is the real thing to lose.

anchor_text: how quote you my folly
summary: 'Quote' here means 'observe' or 'note down' -- as in making a marginal annotation. Thurio asks how Valentine reads, or marks, his folly; Valentine says he can see it inscribed in Thurio's jerkin (his jacket). The word has nothing to do with repeating someone else's words; it is the older sense of 'to observe carefully,' closely related to 'quoth' (said).

anchor_text: he is a kind of chameleon
summary: The chameleon was proverbially believed to feed on air and to change colour at will. Valentine calls the thin-complected Thurio a chameleon because he has just 'changed colour' (gone pale or red with anger), while Thurio's sharp comeback -- he would sooner feed on Valentine's blood than breathe his air -- keeps the animal metaphor alive. The chameleon-as-flatterer, feeding on the empty air of favour, was a commonplace Elizabethan image for a courtier without substance.
detail: The belief that chameleons lived on nothing but air is ancient (Pliny the Elder, Natural History 8.51) and remained standard in English natural history through the 16th century. The creature's colour-changing made it a byword for inconstancy -- an ironic charge to level at Thurio while the genuinely Protean Proteus is about to enter. Speed will echo the image in the next act when he catalogues the signs of Valentine's lovesickness.

anchor_text: fine volley of words, gentlemen, and quickly shot off
summary: Silvia uses a tennis or artillery metaphor: the rapid trading of insults is a 'volley' (an exchange of shots, or of a tennis ball returned before it bounces). When Valentine says Silvia 'gave the fire' -- pulled the trigger -- he plays on the artillery sense. Thurio 'borrows his wit from your ladyship's looks' is then a compliment with a bite: Silvia's eyes sparked the volley, but Thurio's wit is borrowed ammunition he has already spent. The whole exchange is a miniature wit-combat, or stichomythia.
detail: The tennis-volley and the firearms pun on 'fire' (TLN 646) both belong to the rapid-exchange rhetoric of Elizabethan comic wooing. The tennis pun on 'love' (a score of zero, connected etymologically to l'oeuf, an egg) is used elsewhere in the play (Speed, 2.5), but here the sport is gunfire from Silvia's eyes -- itself a Petrarchan cliche (the lady's eyes as weapons) turned comic.

anchor_text: exchequer of words, and, I think, no other treasure
summary: The Exchequer was England's royal treasury -- its finance ministry. 'Bare liveries' means thin, threadbare servants' uniforms, signalling a lord too poor to clothe his household properly; 'bare words' doubles back to those empty wages. The joke: Thurio talks richly but is actually mean, both in wit and in cash.

anchor_text: We have convers'd and spent our hours together
summary: 'Convers'd' does not mean 'talked' in the modern sense; it means 'kept company with' or 'lived alongside.' anchor_text: His head unmellowed, but his judgment ripe
summary: 'Unmellowed' (not yet ripened, not yet grey) means Proteus is still young, his hair still dark rather than the silver of age. 'Ripe' is the contrasting term from the same fruit-metaphor: his judgment has matured early, even though his head has not yet been 'mellowed' by years. The couplet ('His years but young, but his experience old; / His head unmellowed, but his judgment ripe') is a studied paradox, or antithesis -- a rhetorical figure praising precocious wisdom.
detail: The repeated 'but' (called antithesis or adversative pairing) is a stock figure of Ciceronian praise-oratory, here used to build Proteus up as a young man already in command of old-man qualities. Shakespeare will undercut all this praise within fifty lines, when Proteus soliloquizes that he intends to betray his friend.

anchor_text: his mistresss Did hold his eyes lock'd in her crystal looks
summary: The image of a lover's eyes imprisoned in his lady's are a standard Petrarchan conceit: the mistress's gaze is crystalline (both transparent-beautiful and reflective), and the lover cannot look away. Silvia picks up the metaphor sharply -- if Julia's eyes imprison Proteus, 'he should be blind' by now. The exchange is a mini-debate about the paradoxes of love: Love is blind (Cupid is conventionally blindfolded), yet love also famously 'hath twenty pair of eyes' (TLN 702).

anchor_text: Love hath twenty pair of eyes
summary: Cupid, god of love, is conventionally portrayed as blind or blindfolded -- the lover cannot see the faults of the beloved. Valentine turns the cliche on Thurio: 'Love hath twenty pair of eyes' is a jest that Love can see perfectly well when it suits him (Proteus found his way here despite Julia's supposed hold), but is conveniently blind to homely objects like Thurio himself. The immediate follow-up 'Upon a homely object Love can wink' makes the insult explicit.
detail: The blindness of Cupid derives ultimately from Ovid and was elaborated in Renaissance emblem books (Andrea Alciato, Emblemata, 1531). 'Wink' in this period means to shut one eye or both -- to look away or pretend not to see. Valentine is punning: Cupid can see twenty ways at once, but when faced with Thurio, even blind Love would close its eyes.

Valentine has already been Silvia's 'servant' (Silvia opens the scene calling him 'Servant'); here he asks her to take Proteus into the same relationship. anchor_text: I have done penance for contemning Love
summary: Valentine describes his conversion from love-sceptic to lover in the language of religious penance: he 'contemned' (scorned and rejected) Love, Love took revenge with 'bitter fasts,' 'penitential groans,' and sleepless nights, and now there is 'no woe to his correction' (no punishment like Love's). The speech is a Petrarchan catalogue of the lover's sufferings, here cast as just punishment for former unbelief. Love is personified as a powerful 'lord' whose correction must be endured and then obeyed.

The speech mirrors, at a comic distance, the scene in which Valentine earlier scorned his love-struck friend Proteus (1.1): Valentine has now become what he derided.

anchor_text: let her be a principality, Sovereign to all the creatures on the earth
summary: In the medieval and Renaissance understanding of the celestial hierarchy, 'principalities' were one rank of angels -- powerful beings set above ordinary creatures and below archangels. Valentine, unable to convince Proteus that Silvia is 'divine,' asks at minimum that she be ranked as a 'principality,' sovereign over all earthly things. The praise escalates through the scene from 'earthly paragon' (Proteus) to 'heavenly saint' to 'angel-like perfection' (TLN 673); 'principality' is Valentine's compromise position, still superhuman even if not quite divine.
detail: The standard angelic hierarchy (from Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, 5th century, widely circulated in the Renaissance) placed Principalities as the seventh of nine orders. The word carried both this theological resonance and a plain sense of 'sovereign power.' Valentine is doing theology-of-love: if not a saint, then at least a ruling angel.

anchor_text: She shall be dignified with this high honour
summary: Valentine's mockery of Proteus's mistress Julia turns into an elaborate hyperbole: Silvia is so far above all other women that Julia's greatest honour would be to carry Silvia's train (the trailing hem of a great lady's gown) so that even the ground might not 'steal a kiss' from Silvia's dress. The figure -- even the earth is too base to touch her garment -- then turns into a cosmological conceit: if earth grew proud from that kiss, it would refuse to nourish the summer flowers, and winter would last forever. Valentine has been infected by Petrarchan hyperbole.

The joke is that Valentine is parodying the very poetry he now sincerely believes: Proteus's flat rebuttal ('Why, Valentine, what braggardism is this?') is the comic corrective.

anchor_text: As twenty seas, if all their sand were pearl, The water nectar, and the rocks pure gold
summary: Valentine compares his 'jewel' Silvia to a fabulous wealth: if twenty seas had sand of pearl, water of nectar (the drink of the gods), and rocks of solid gold, he would still be richer having her. anchor_text: O sweet-suggesting Love! if thou hast sinn'd
summary: 'Suggesting' here does not mean 'proposing an idea' but carries the older sense of tempting or inciting to sin — the vocabulary of diabolic temptation. It is a stock figure of contempt in the love poetry of the period, not a considered judgment.

'Ethiope' (Latin Aethiops, from Greek for 'burnt-face') was the period's generic term for a sub-Saharan African, and 'black' or 'swarthy' was its opposite of 'fair.' The figure appears repeatedly in Shakespeare: in A Midsummer Night's Dream Lysander, enchanted by the potion, dismisses Hermia as 'Ethiope' (3.2); Portia in The Merchant of Venice compares the Prince of Morocco's dark skin to unfair contrast. The cruel irony here is that Proteus is using the language of beauty-praise to demean a woman he swore he loved with 'twenty thousand soul-confirming oaths' (TLN 892) — the very extravagance of the dismissal exposes his bad faith.

anchor_text: Thou common friend, that's without faith or love
summary: 'Common' here means available to all, promiscuous, debased — not the standard 'ordinary' sense. Valentine means Proteus is a friend to anyone and therefore a true friend to nobody: his friendship is as worthless as a 'common woman' (a prostitute).

anchor_text: The private wound is deep'st. O time most curst! 'Mongst all foes that a friend should be the worst
summary: Valentine's couplet uses an epigram (a pointed, memorable summing-up) to crystallise his grief: betrayal by a friend hurts more than any public enemy could. The paradox — that the closest friend becomes the worst foe — is the emotional core of the whole play, and it reaches the reader as a general truth, not just a personal complaint.
detail: The sentiment is proverbial in Elizabethan writing; compare the Latin 'Inimicus homo, amicus simulans' (an enemy imitating a friend) and Sidney's reflection on false friends in Arcadia. The couplet form signals finality, a closing-off: Valentine has said everything he can say. Dramatically it prepares Proteus's repentance, which must be equal to this articulate grief.

anchor_text: Then I am paid; And once again I do receive thee honest
summary: Valentine's instant acceptance of Proteus's repentance — and his declaration 'All that was mine in Silvia I give thee' — enacts the Renaissance ideal of perfect male friendship, in which a true friend values the bond above all else, including his own love. The gesture has troubled readers and audiences for centuries.

anchor_text: Who by repentance is not satisfied Is nor of heaven nor earth
summary: Valentine is applying the Christian doctrine that sincere repentance (penitence) satisfies both God and the offended party: if heaven forgives the truly penitent, so must an earthly friend. The allusion grounds his forgiveness of Proteus in standard Protestant theology about contrition.
detail: The Geneva Bible glosses the parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32) on exactly this logic: the father runs to embrace the returning son, asking nothing further once true sorrow is shown. Valentine's argument — 'by penitence the Eternal's wrath's appeas'd' (TLN 2108) — draws on the Protestant consensus that genuine contrition, without further penalty, restores the offender. 'The Eternal' is a circumlocution for God. The speed of Proteus's forgiveness is arguably more doctrinally coherent than it first appears, though critics note that Valentine's theology conveniently serves his own emotional need to reunite with his friend.

anchor_text: this is the ring I gave to Julia
summary: The exchange of rings was a binding pledge of betrothal in Elizabethan practice. Proteus gave Julia a ring when they parted (2.2); he later sent another ring to Silvia via his disguised page 'Sebastian' (Julia herself). Julia now produces both: the one Proteus gave her as a love-token, and the one he sent Silvia as a false token. The double ring exposes his double betrayal at a glance.
detail: In Elizabethan and earlier custom a ring exchanged between lovers carried quasi-contractual force: Proteus's ring to Julia was effectively a pledge of fidelity. His attempt to recycle a love-token by sending a ring to Silvia through the very woman he had pledged it to is the concrete symbol of his inconstancy. The two rings give Julia her recognition scene: presenting them in sequence, she moves from 'Sebastian' the page to Julia the woman. The same ring device is central to the recognition scenes of The Merchant of Venice and Much Ado About Nothing.

sources.name: Swinburne, A Treatise of Spousals
sources.citation: Henry Swinburne, A Treatise of Spousals, or Matrimonial Contracts (written c. 1600, published 1686), on the exchange of tokens as evidence of pre-contract in Elizabethan law.

The summary correctly tracks the two-ring device as staged in the text; the quasi-contractual force of a betrothal ring in Elizabethan custom is defensible and explains why Proteus's ring to Julia is incriminating, not merely sentimental.

anchor_text: Behold her that gave aim to all thy oaths
summary: 'Gave aim' is an archery term: the 'aim-giver' stood near the target and called back to the archer whether shots were high, low, or wide, so the archer could correct. Julia is saying she was the target of all Proteus's vows of love — the one his oaths were aimed at — and she is still here to witness what he has done with them.

The archery gloss of 'gave aim' — to stand near the target and report results to the archer — is OED-attested and makes excellent sense here: Julia was the target Proteus's vows were directed at and she is still present to witness their deviation.

anchor_text: How oft hast thou with perjury cleft the root
summary: 'Cleft the root' means split something to the core — 'perjury cleft the root' is perjury that cuts down to the very foundation of trust. The image is of an axe splitting a tree at its base, destroying it utterly.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2129

'Cleft the root' as splitting to the very foundation is a natural reading of 'cleave' in the sense of violent splitting; the tree-root image for the foundation of trust is consistent with Shakespeare's usage elsewhere and the annotation does not overreach.

anchor_text: It is the lesser blot, modesty finds, Women to change their shapes than men their minds
summary: Julia distinguishes between her disguise (a woman changing outward 'shape' by cross-dressing) and Proteus's betrayal (a man changing his inner 'mind' — his love, his loyalty). Her disguise was 'a disguise of love' (line 2133), driven by faithfulness, not inconstancy; his transformations are moral, not sartorial.
detail: The couplet is Julia's most pointed rhetorical move: it sets the Protean metaphor (Proteus's name, his nature) against a counter-proof — she has changed shape for love, he has changed character against love. The argument echoes the play's central naming device: Proteus the shape-changer has changed his mind where it matters, while Julia, having changed only her clothes, has remained herself throughout. The paradox that disguise can be an act of constancy is a favourite comic device of Shakespeare's heroines in male dress (Viola, Rosalind, Portia).

sources.name: Leech, Arden 2 Two Gentlemen
sources.citation: Clifford Leech, ed., The Two Gentlemen of Verona, Arden Shakespeare, 2nd series (1969), note on 5.4.108-111.

Julia's argument — that changing outward shape (disguise from faithfulness) is a lesser fault than changing inner mind (betrayal) — is exactly what the text argues, and the connection to the Proteus naming device is a mainstream reading, not an overreading.

anchor_text: A prize, a prize, a prize
summary: 'Prize' in this context is a nautical and military term for a captured vessel or prisoner — something seized as spoils. The outlaw is announcing that the Duke and Thurio have been captured as valuable prisoners. Valentine immediately overrules him.

anchor_text: Come not within the measure of my wrath
summary: 'Measure' here is a fencing term for the distance at which a sword can reach. 'Within the measure of my wrath' means within sword's reach — Valentine is telling Thurio to stay back or be cut down.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2154

The fencing sense of 'measure' as sword's reach is OED-attested and is the right reading in this threat context; it is a straightforward archaic-vocabulary gloss, not an overreach.

anchor_text: we will include all jars With triumphs, mirth, and rare solemnity
summary: 'Jars' means quarrels or discords (as in 'jarring' notes). 'Triumphs' here does not mean military victories but festive public celebrations — processions, masques, revels. The Duke promises to wrap up all the quarrels of the play in a festival: the word 'solemnity' means a formal, dignified ceremony (not a gloomy one).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2187
Onions s.v. 'jar,' 'triumph' sense 3, and 'solemnity' are all real entries that accurately support the glosses of discord, festive pageant, and formal ceremony.

All three glosses ('jars' as discords, 'triumphs' as festive pageants, 'solemnity' as formal ceremony rather than gloom) are standard Elizabethan senses and are clearly operative in this conventional comic-ending speech.

anchor_text: I think the boy hath grace in him; he blushes
summary: The Duke sees 'Sebastian' (actually Julia in disguise) blush — a sign he reads as girlish modesty but mistakes for boyish embarrassment. Valentine's answer, 'more grace than boy,' hints to the audience that the 'page' is a woman, without yet explaining this to the Duke. The unmasking of Julia's disguise is deferred to the road-walk off-stage, preserving decorum for the women of the play.
